cues.text: I would uphold the challenged Hawaii law because, as Justice Jackson shows in Part three of her opinion, it is a modern-day analogue of colonial and founding era laws that similarly prohibited carrying firearms onto private property without the owner's affirmative consent.
The “how” is identical: The new law, just like the old ones, sets a default rule against gun carry that a private landowner may reverse.
Both sets of laws respond to the dangers and harms that someone with a gun can cause on another person's property.
That the old laws had a special (though by no means exclusive) concern with poaching does not matter.
“The regulatory challenges posed by firearms today are not always the same as those that preoccupied” earlier generations.
The key question is whether the challenged regulation is “consistent with the principles that underpin our regulatory tradition.”

Here, the challenged law is consistent with those principles because it reflects, as the old laws did, the perceived “abuses, damages and inconveniences” that can be caused by persons carrying guns “on other people's lands.”
That conclusion is enough for me to resolve this case, without addressing Bruen's step-one inquiry or the use at step two of Louisiana's Black Code.
